title: Rattle and Hums
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien takes on the common objection that explicit teaching and the science of learning 'wouldn't work in my subject area', using more than a decade of Humanities teaching in Victoria to argue it applies everywhere. His premise is that learning runs on attention, rehearsal and retrieval regardless of subject, so what changes is how checking and modelling look, not whether they occur. He diagnoses why Humanities teams drift toward choose-your-own-adventure inquiry tasks: the faculty bundles disparate subjects, is often taught by non-specialists, and professional learning rarely models explicit teaching outside maths and English, so teachers have no schema for it. He then walks through accounting, business management, economics, history and legal studies, showing how mini whiteboards, gradual release (I do, we do, you do), cause-and-effect checks, primary-source questioning and short invented legal cases can all be used for checks for understanding. The piece warns that skipping background knowledge leaves students able to write but with nothing to write about.
points: Learning depends on attention, rehearsal and retrieval over time in every subject, so explicit teaching changes form across disciplines but not in principle.
Humanities teams often default to open-ended inquiry because teachers are generalists, so students refine copying from Wikipedia or AI instead of learning content.
Teachers lack mental models for explicit teaching in their own subject because professional learning is pitched at maths and English, and skills do not transfer automatically.

Concrete subject examples (accounting equation on mini whiteboards, I do/we do/you do for business strategies, source analysis in history, invented mini cases in legal studies) show how to chunk and check content.
Background knowledge is what students need to write, so stripping it away for generic literacy skills leaves them with nothing to write about.
quotes: Learning doesn’t discriminate based on subject. Learning will happen through the process of attention, rehearsal and retrieval over time.
This is the exact same process as explicitly teaching a concept and then checking for understanding, yet it is occurring in a completely different way.
Instead you build students who understand how to write, but have nothing to write about as they do not know anything about the world around them.

We also know that skills are not directly transferable and therefore just because you see an example problem pair presented as a strategy in math does not meant that a teacher of humanities will be able to transfer how the same logic and structure would apply to their subject.
The pre-existing beliefs of what their subject is and the purpose of learning it can be the greatest challenge to overcome.
Economics as a subject area is a very cause and effect in nature which works amazingly for checks for understanding.

The upside of this with explicit teaching is that it lends itself amazingly to the gradual release of responsibility as each of those 13 items (which in this example are management strategies to respond to key performance indicators) procedurally apply in the exact same way.
